data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms as a methodological rule based on the asymmetry of risk, not as an inductive inference of future probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly stated that choosing a better-corroborated theory implies a belief in its higher future reliability or probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference cannot be distinguished from inductive habit when applied to concrete scientific decisions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the framework requires a guarantee of success to justify any preference, rendering 'educated guesswork' insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which cannot be made more probable by past tests) and the pragmatic decision of which theory to adopt for action. The mechanism is a 'critical preference': since all theories are conjectures, the rational agent chooses the one that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification because rejecting it in favor of a less-tested theory would increase the risk of error without any compensating logical gain. This relies on the informational content of the theory rather than its probability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
